summary:
Thüringen stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and the state government cannot remove that federal floor.

No trans-specific safety finding was documented for Thüringen. The sources record no prosecution, assault or enforcement action against a trans visitor in the state, so the risk picture there rests on political posture and on the exposures that apply across Germany.

In the state election of 1 September 2024, AfD Thüringen, classified by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution as right-wing extremist, took 32.8% of the vote, ahead of the CDU at 23.4%, the BSW at 15.8% in its first state election, Die Linke at 13.1% and the SPD at 6.1%. The CDU, BSW and SPD then formed the first 'Brombeerkoalition' under minister-president Mario Voigt, a minority cabinet without its own Landtag majority. Within that configuration the AfD fraction moved to have the existing ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools consistently enforced and proposed dismantling the state's equality machinery. Formal, multi-layered institutional hostility to gender policy in Thüringen rests on this parliamentary arithmetic.

On 2 June 2026 Thüringen co-signed an initiative from Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after the 'Liebich case', framing anti-abuse amendments alongside stronger recognition of trans and intersex people. The Self-Determination Act itself, in force since 1 November 2024, lets adults change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, and a 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019, though only on a doctor's statement confirming intersex status. Three state governments can call for federal change; they cannot enact it.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans person anywhere in Germany, and it applies equally on Thuringian territory. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The outcome has gone both ways in documented cases: in August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich would serve an 18-month sentence at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake, and DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had instead been transferred to a men's prison despite legal registration as a woman, authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility.

Airport entry carries a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024 in which, on her account reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment. Screening equipment and officer discretion at entry points are national, not Thuringian, variables.
tangentialFactors:
The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule requiring separation by legal sex, reports that placement matching a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only exceptionally, and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all. Thüringen's own correctional provisions on this point are not described in the sources.

In the earlier Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates. Trans people held in Berlin have an official information page from the Berlin prison service setting out rules and contacts across the city's facilities; no equivalent Thuringian page appears in the inventory.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested nationally since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument about registered trans women's access, with reporting from Berlin on how leisure venues handle trans women after the new law. Leisure operators in Thüringen work under the same national statute and the same unresolved industry guidance.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006, and a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison and fines of €30,000 since May 2020. Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025: in June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
localsOnly:
The Thuringian Landtag already carries a ban on gender-inclusive language in schools. The AfD fraction's motion 'Keine Gendersprache an Thüringer Schulen' demands that the Landtag's existing ban be consistently implemented and asserts that schools must not be a socio-political experimental field. The same fraction proposed dismantling the state's equality machinery, a proposal aimed at the administrative channels residents use to raise discrimination complaints.

The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the federal Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. That finding concerns federal administration, while the Thuringian school ban operates through a Landtag decision and affects teachers, pupils and school communication inside the state.

Residents of Thüringen are governed on identity documents by the Self-Determination Act and the 'divers' marker rather than by any state instrument, and the state's contribution to that regime has been to co-sign, with Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt, a call for anti-abuse amendments to the federal law together with stronger trans and intersex recognition. The three-state initiative was reported on 2 June 2026; whether it has moved beyond a joint position is not described in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no trans-specific safety finding was documented for Thüringen, and the absence of a recorded incident is not a finding of safety. The inventory contains no Thuringian prosecution, assault, police or administrative data on trans people, so enforcement of the state's posture cannot be assessed from these sources.

Not sourced: whether the Thuringian ban on gender-inclusive language in schools has produced complaints, court challenges or documented effects on trans pupils; whether the proposal to dismantle the state's equality machinery advanced beyond a motion; and the current composition and budget of that machinery.

Not sourced: any Thuringian prison-service instruction on housing trans prisoners, any intake-review practice in Thuringian facilities, and whether a Thuringian equivalent of the Berlin prison service's trans information page exists. The placement cases in the inventory originate in Saxony and in earlier federal reporting, not in Thüringen.

Unresolved: the operative status of the Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thüringen initiative to tighten the Self-Determination Act as of the dossier date, and whether any federal bill followed the 2 June 2026 joint call.
